title: Books and Reading
goal: describe your reaction to a book, ask for a suitable recommendation, and handle a bookstore or subscription question.

study.title: Give a reaction with enough meaning

runs.text: “I'm reading a mystery” names the kind of book. “It's about two sisters looking for a missing letter” gives its basic subject. You can add what you think without revealing the ending.
How's that novel you started?

turns.speaker: Casey

runs.text: I'm really enjoying it. The chapters are short, but a lot happens.

turns.en: I'm really enjoying it. The chapters are short, but a lot happens.

runs.text: Is it scary?

turns.speaker: Casey

runs.text: A little tense, more than scary. I want to know what happens next.

turns.en: A little tense, more than scary. I want to know what happens next.

runs.text: Would you recommend it?

turns.speaker: Casey

runs.text: Yes, if you like mysteries. Don't read the description on the back too closely—it gives away part of the story.

turns.en: Yes, if you like mysteries. Don't read the description on the back too closely—it gives away part of the story.

blocks.caption: Give a reaction with enough meaning · Drew & Casey

runs.text: A
novel
is a long work of fiction. A
mystery
centers on something to be explained, often a crime. A
biography
tells a person's life; an
autobiography
is written by that person.
Fiction
presents invented stories;
nonfiction
presents factual subjects, though you can still question a writer's claims.
Useful reactions include:

rows.text: It makes me eager to read what comes next.
It kept me on the edge of my seat.
I felt strong suspense or excitement.
Reading it took effort or felt difficult.

runs.text: You can also say exactly what you mean: “I liked the characters, but the ending disappointed me.” You do not need an idiom to give a good reaction. “Hard going” might refer to difficult language, slow progress, or heavy subject matter; explain which you mean.

Someone else can love a book you dislike. “I can see why you liked it. I thought the middle was too slow” expresses both recognition and disagreement. You can be more direct: “It didn't work for me at all.” Add a reason if you want to keep the conversation going.

turns.speaker: Customer

runs.text: I'm looking for a book for a long flight. Something short and funny, preferably fiction.

turns.en: I'm looking for a book for a long flight. Something short and funny, preferably fiction.

turns.speaker: Bookseller

runs.text: How about this collection of short stories? Each one takes about ten minutes to read.

turns.en: How about this collection of short stories? Each one takes about ten minutes to read.

turns.speaker: Customer

runs.text: That sounds good. Is it available in paperback?

turns.en: That sounds good. Is it available in paperback?

turns.speaker: Bookseller

runs.text: We have the paperback here for twelve dollars.

turns.en: We have the paperback here for twelve dollars.

runs.text: I'll take it.

blocks.caption: Choose something in a bookstore · Customer & Bookseller

runs.text: These price and reading-time estimates belong to this fictional scene.
Paperback
has a flexible paper cover;
hardcover
has a stiff cover. “I'm just browsing, thanks” means you are looking without needing help yet. If a book is
out of stock
, the shop does not currently have it available. Ask, “Can you order it?” and “When would it arrive?” without assuming the answer.
“I skim the headlines first” means you read quickly for the main points. “I flip through the magazine” means you look through its pages without necessarily reading everything. A
subscription
gives continuing access or delivery under stated terms.
Renew
continues it for a new period: “How much would it cost to renew?”
These books are invented for this exercise:
The Last Ferry:
a 180-page mystery; tense, with short chapters; paperback, $14.
Small Accidents:
funny short stories; paperback, $12.
A Life in Gardens:
a long biography about a landscape designer; hardcover, $28.
Partner wants short, funny fiction for a trip. Recommend
Small Accidents
and explain the fit. Partner then says, “Actually, I'd rather have a mystery.” Change your recommendation. Possible response: “Then try
The Last Ferry
. It's a short mystery with lots of suspense.”

Fictional reading facts: you liked the characters and found the first half exciting, but the ending felt rushed. Tell a friend without giving away the ending. Partner: “Really? I loved the ending.” Continue with your own view rather than automatically agreeing.
Possibility: “I liked the characters, but the ending was a letdown for me. I wanted more explanation.” Another sensible response is “I can see that. I still thought it felt rushed.”

Role facts: the book you want is out of stock. Staff: “We can order it. It would arrive next Wednesday.” You need it by Monday. Explain that the arrival is too late and ask about another format or a different book. Staff: “The e-book is available today.” You prefer a physical book; decline and ask for a different recommendation.
Then ask about a magazine renewal when you do not know the price. “What would it cost to renew for a year?” is enough; do not invent a price.
Solo route:

read the partner cues aloud, answer, and switch to the alternative preference. Cover the table and explain two reactions in plain words. Check whether your recommendation uses the supplied facts and whether your reaction tells the listener what you actually liked or disliked.

note: Page-turner は続きが気になる本という表現です。自分の感想を具体化し、相手の好みや読む時間に合う本を尋ねます。
